blocks.content: Given J&K's deep multi-religious heritage (Chapter 20), its pilgrimage sites form a distinct and heavily tested chapter of their own, spanning Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and Buddhist traditions.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Covers the historical and cultural significance of the Amarnath Yatra.
Details major pilgrimage and religious sites across Jammu & Kashmir.
Provides quick revision highlights for competitive examination preparation.

blocks.content: The Amarnath Cave, located at approximately 3,888 m in the Himalayas of south Kashmir, houses a naturally forming ice stalagmite ('Shiva Lingam') that waxes and wanes with the seasons, revered as a manifestation of Lord Shiva and forming the destination of the annual Amarnath Yatra, one of Hinduism's most significant Himalayan pilgrimages.

The Yatra typically takes place over several weeks each year (usually between late June/July and August, timed around the Hindu month of Shravan), following two traditional routes — the shorter, steeper Baltal route (via Sonamarg) and the longer, more traditional Pahalgam route (via the Lidder Valley and Sheshnag Lake, Chapter 4) — with pilgrims registering in advance and the Yatra managed by the Shri Amarnath Shrine Board under significant security and logistical arrangements given the route's high-altitude terrain and periodic security concerns.
The Yatra draws several hundred thousand pilgrims in a typical year and represents a major annual logistical, economic and security undertaking for the J&K UT administration.

★ EXAM POINT: Shri Amarnath Shrine Board (SASB) is the statutory body managing the Yatra — a frequently tested administrative-body name alongside the pilgrimage's two route names (Baltal and Pahalgam) and its Shravan-month timing.

cells: One of India's most visited Hindu pilgrimage sites, dedicated to the Goddess Vaishno Devi; managed by the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board; draws millions of pilgrims annually, making it one of the highest-footfall religious sites in India
Revered Muslim shrine on Dal Lake's shore, believed to house a relic associated with the Prophet Muhammad
Shrine of Sheikh Noor-ud-din Noorani ('Nund Rishi'), founder of Kashmir's indigenous Rishi Sufi order (Chapter 20)
Historic Sufi shrine associated with Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani (Chapter 6)
Associated with the visit of Guru Hargobind Sahib, the sixth Sikh Guru, a significant Sikh pilgrimage site within the Valley
Primarily Ladakh UT (Hemis, Thiksey, Alchi monasteries etc.)

While Buddhist monastic heritage is now predominantly associated with the separate Ladakh UT, it forms part of the shared historical religious landscape of the erstwhile combined state, given Buddhism's early presence in ancient Kashmir itself (Chapter 5)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Vaishno Devi (Jammu division) is one of the highest-footfall pilgrimage sites in all of India by annual visitor numbers — a frequently tested comparative statistic distinguishing it clearly from the smaller-scale (though highly significant) Amarnath Yatra.

items: Amarnath Cave (~3,888 m): naturally forming ice Shiva Lingam; Yatra managed by the Shri Amarnath Shrine Board; two routes — Baltal (shorter) and Pahalgam (longer, traditional).
Vaishno Devi Shrine (Trikuta Hills, near Katra): one of India's highest-footfall pilgrimage sites; managed by the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board.
Hazratbal Shrine (Srinagar): believed to house a Prophet Muhammad relic.
Charar-e-Sharief: shrine of Nund Rishi, founder of Kashmir's Rishi Sufi order.
Gurdwara Chatti Padshahi, Srinagar: associated with the sixth Sikh Guru, Guru Hargobind Sahib.
